body.back: Tourism that meets the needs of present tourists and host communities while protecting the environment and opportunities for future generations.
Environmental, social (socio-cultural) and economic sustainability.
body.front: What are the three pillars of sustainable tourism?

body.back: Responsible travel to natural areas that conserves the environment, sustains the well-being of local people and involves education.
The total amount of greenhouse gases, especially carbon dioxide, produced by an activity, person, organisation or product.
Paying for projects, such as tree planting, that reduce greenhouse gases to balance emissions produced by travel.
Pollution (air, water, noise, litter) and damage to habitats or landscapes, for example erosion of footpaths or coral damage.
body.front: Give two negative environmental impacts of tourism.

body.back: When money spent by tourists leaves the destination, for example profits going to foreign-owned hotels or tour operators.
Money spent by tourists is re-spent in the local economy, creating further income and jobs.
When too many tourists visit a destination at once, causing pressure on resources, congestion and a poorer experience for visitors and residents.
body.hint: Too many people, too little space.

body.back: A popular attraction or location that draws very large numbers of tourists, often causing congestion and damage.
Recycle waste and use energy-saving measures, such as low-energy lighting, or reuse towels to save water.
body.front: Give two ways to reduce the environmental impact of a hotel.

body.back: It creates jobs and income, and funds improved infrastructure and services such as roads, schools and healthcare.
body.front: Give two ways tourism can benefit local communities.

body.back: Tourism owned and managed by local people so that they make decisions and receive most of the benefits.
Strategies used to control tourist numbers and behaviour, such as quotas, entry fees, zoning and guided tours, to reduce negative impacts.
body.front: What is meant by visitor management?

body.back: Loss of local traditions or culture, or conflict, when tourist behaviour or commercialisation changes the way of life of host communities.
body.front: Define a negative socio-cultural impact of tourism.

body.back: The activity of people travelling to and staying in places outside their usual environment for leisure, business or other purposes, for not more than one year.
Tourism where people travel within their own country, e.g. a French resident taking a holiday in France.
Tourism where visitors travel into a country from another country, e.g. a Japanese tourist visiting Kenya (from Kenya's point of view).
Tourism where residents of a country travel to another country, e.g. a Kenyan resident taking a holiday in Spain.
Travel for relaxation, enjoyment and pleasure in free time, such as beach holidays, sightseeing and theme park visits.
Travel for work-related purposes, such as meetings, conferences, exhibitions, incentive trips and training events.
Travel to visit friends and relatives, often staying in their homes rather than paid accommodation.
Travel to experience the heritage, history, art, traditions and way of life of a destination, e.g. museums, festivals and historic sites.
Travel involving physical activity, challenge and some risk in natural environments, e.g. white-water rafting, trekking or bungee jumping.
Responsible travel to natural areas that conserves the environment, respects local people and educates visitors.
Travel to improve health or wellbeing, such as spa breaks, wellness retreats or medical treatment abroad.
Stress from work or daily life and the desire to relax; wanting to escape routine or bad weather at home.

body.back: Attractive climate and scenery; attractions, culture, facilities and good value for money that draw visitors to the destination.
body.front: Give two pull factors of a destination
body.hint: Pull = pulls you towards a place

body.back: To relax and rest; to enjoy new experiences, activities or entertainment; to spend quality time with family and friends.

topic: Types of tourism & reasons to travel

body.q: A family from Manchester travels to Spain for a two-week holiday. Which type of tourism is this?
body.why: Outbound tourism is when residents of a country travel to another country, so from the UK perspective a trip to Spain is outbound.

body.q: A tourist from Japan visits Kenya on a safari holiday. From Kenya's perspective, which type of tourism is this?
body.why: Inbound tourism describes visitors arriving in a country from another country, so Kenya receives an inbound tourist.

body.q: A couple from Sydney spends a long weekend in the Blue Mountains, also in Australia. Which type of tourism does this describe?
body.why: Domestic tourism is when people travel within their own country.

o: Attending an international trade fair in Dubai
Taking a cruise around the Caribbean
Going on a skiing holiday in Switzerland
body.q: Which of the following is an example of business tourism?
body.why: Business tourism involves travel for work-related purposes such as conferences, meetings, exhibitions and trade fairs.

body.q: A group of friends travels to Rio de Janeiro to experience Carnival. Which type of tourism does this best describe?
body.why: Cultural tourism involves travelling to experience a destination's festivals, traditions, heritage and way of life.

body.q: A traveller goes to Thailand for a dental procedure that costs less than at home and combines it with a few days on the beach. Which type of tourism is the main reason for this trip?
body.why: Medical tourism is travelling abroad to receive medical or dental treatment, often for lower cost or shorter waiting times.

o: Wanting to escape a stressful daily routine
A famous landmark in another country
body.q: Which of the following is a 'push' factor that might motivate someone to travel on holiday?
body.why: Push factors are personal motivations within the traveller, such as the need to relax, whereas the other options are features of destinations that pull visitors.

o: A warm climate and sandy beaches
A tourist feeling tired of work
A person needing a break from study
A family wanting to spend time together
body.q: Which of the following is the best example of a 'pull' factor for a destination?
body.why: Pull factors are attractions or qualities of a destination, such as climate and scenery, that draw tourists to it.

body.q: A person travels to a different city for the weekend specifically to attend their cousin's wedding. Which reason for travel is this?
body.why: Travel to attend family events or see relatives is classified as visiting friends and relatives (VFR).

body.q: A tour operator offers trips to a rainforest where small groups stay in locally owned lodges, and part of the fee supports wildlife conservation. Which type of tourism is this?
body.why: Eco-tourism involves responsible travel to natural areas that protects the environment and benefits local communities.
